---

## Synthesis: Test-Suite Speed and AI Coding Agents (2025–2026)

---

### 1. The Verification Bottleneck — Is It Real?

**Well-supported (multiple independent sources):**

- **Leonardo Stern / Agoda via InfoQ** (2026-03): "The bottleneck has shifted upstream to specification and verification because these areas require human judgment." Agoda's finding: AI boosts individual output but project-level velocity gains are modest — coding was never the constraint. Source: [InfoQ: Agoda AI Code Bottleneck](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/03/agoda-ai-code-bottleneck/)

- **Faros AI data cited by InfoQ**: High-adoption AI teams "completed 21% more tasks and merged 98% more pull requests, yet PR review time increased 91%." The output doubled; verification burden nearly doubled. Same URL.

- **Abhishek Ray / Opslane** (blog): "AI-written tests have the same blind spots as AI-written code." Three-part verification pattern recommended: real test suites + human-specified acceptance criteria defined *before* AI writes code + a separate agent-based adversarial verification pass. Source: [Opslane: Verification Is the Next Bottleneck](https://www.opslane.com/blog/verification-bottleneck/)

- **METR study (2025), cited by Opslane**: Developers believed AI made them 20% faster; measured result was 19% *slower* on real tasks. Confidence: anecdotal (one study, contested methodology, but widely cited).

- **DORA 2024 "verification tax" framing**, cited by Opslane: time saved writing code is re-spent auditing it. Well-supported (Accelerate report has broad practitioner uptake), but the "verification tax" label appears to be Opslane's coinage applied to DORA data, not DORA's own term.

---

### 2. Agent Feedback Loop Pattern — Tiered vs. Full-Suite

**Well-supported (primary source, Anthropic's own docs):**

Claude Code's official best-practices guide ([code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices)) does **not** explicitly prescribe tiered loops (fast inner-loop / full-suite pre-commit). Instead it recommends:

- Give the agent *any* verifiable check (tests, build exit code, linter, diff script) so the loop closes autonomously. The check can be a targeted single test, not the whole suite.
- CLAUDE.md example line cited verbatim: `"Prefer running single tests, and not the whole test suite, for performance"` — this is the clearest Anthropic guidance toward targeted/fast inner-loop testing.
- Four escalating gate options: inline prompt, `/goal` condition, Stop hook (deterministic gate), verification subagent (adversarial reviewer). The Stop hook is the strongest — blocks turn-end until the check passes, up to 8 consecutive blocks.
- Adversarial subagent pattern: a second Claude in a fresh context reviews the diff against requirements, not the reasoning that produced it. Recommended before marking unattended runs done.

**Implied tiered pattern (not explicitly named as such):** The guidance to "run single tests for performance" in inner loops, combined with Stop hooks for pre-commit gates, maps onto the tiered-loop model in practice — but Anthropic does not publish it as a named pattern.

---

### 3. Concrete Techniques — What Practitioners Advocate

**Go test caching (moderately well-supported):**
- [Rotational Labs: Speeding Up Go Tests](https://rotational.io/blog/speeding-up-go-tests/) and [bjorn.now Go test cache on CI](https://bjorn.now/blog/2025/07/07/working-with-gos-test-cache-on-ci/): caching `GOCACHE` on CI is an easy win. Key caveat: ~10% of tests may not cache as expected in complex codebases; black-box integration tests hitting APIs can cache incorrectly. Known Go issue: ModTime-dependent cache misses on CI ([golang/go#58571](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/58571)).
- `-short` flag and affected-test selection are not covered in these sources with practitioner case studies; their use is implied but anecdotal.

**Shifting test pyramid shape (anecdotal, vendor-influenced):**
- [Bug0 blog](https://bug0.com/blog/software-testing-strategies) and [Frontiers journal: Test Pyramid 2.0](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/artificial-intelligence/articles/10.3389/frai.2025.1695965/full) argue the pyramid should become a "trapezoid" — more E2E, fewer integration tests — because AI agents can run thousands of parallel browser sessions cheaply. E2E cost dropped an order of magnitude. Confidence: low-to-medium; driven by AI testing vendors; limited independent empirical data.

**Structural enforcement over advisory checks:**
- Opslane and the search aggregate data both note: "36% of practitioners using AI code generation skip QA entirely" — structural enforcement (hooks that cannot be bypassed) is the only reliable solution. Corroborated by Claude Code's Stop hook design, which blocks Claude from ending a turn until the check passes.

**Mutation/property testing:** No credible 2025–2026 practitioner source surfaced advocating these as an agent-specific technique. Not covered.

---

### Confidence Summary

| Claim | Confidence |
|---|---|
| Verification (not coding speed) is the binding constraint | High — multiple independent data points (Agoda, Faros AI, DORA framing, Opslane) |
| AI-written tests share AI code blind spots | Medium — reasonable but lacks large empirical study |
| CLAUDE.md guidance: prefer single tests over full suite in inner loop | High — direct primary source, Anthropic |
| Stop hook as deterministic pre-commit gate | High — Anthropic docs |
| Go test caching on CI as a concrete speedup | Medium — practitioner posts, but known cache-miss edge cases |
| Trapezoid over pyramid (more E2E, fewer integration) | Low — vendor-positioned, minimal independent evidence |
| METR: AI made devs 19% slower | Anecdotal — single study, contested |

---

**Actionable summary:** The well-evidenced recommendation is: use targeted tests (single package or affected subset) as the inner-loop signal so the agent iterates quickly; gate pre-commit on a deterministic hook running the full relevant suite; use a separate adversarial subagent as the final reviewer before merging. Anthropic's docs endorse this structure implicitly; no external practitioner source packages it as a named "tiered loop" pattern.

<result>Here is the synthesis. Per-claim, sourced, with confidence flagging.

---

## Synthesis: Test-Suite Speed and AI Coding Agents (2025–2026)

---

### 1. The Verification Bottleneck — Is It Real?

**Well-supported (multiple independent sources):**

- **Leonardo Stern / Agoda via InfoQ** (2026-03): "The bottleneck has shifted upstream to specification and verification because these areas require human judgment." Agoda's finding: AI boosts individual output but project-level velocity gains are modest — coding was never the constraint. Source: [InfoQ: Agoda AI Code Bottleneck](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/03/agoda-ai-code-bottleneck/)

- **Faros AI data cited by InfoQ**: High-adoption AI teams "completed 21% more tasks and merged 98% more pull requests, yet PR review time increased 91%." The output doubled; verification burden nearly doubled. Same URL.

- **Abhishek Ray / Opslane** (blog): "AI-written tests have the same blind spots as AI-written code." Three-part verification pattern recommended: real test suites + human-specified acceptance criteria defined *before* AI writes code + a separate agent-based adversarial verification pass. Source: [Opslane: Verification Is the Next Bottleneck](https://www.opslane.com/blog/verification-bottleneck/)

- **METR study (2025), cited by Opslane**: Developers believed AI made them 20% faster; measured result was 19% *slower* on real tasks. Confidence: anecdotal (one study, contested methodology, but widely cited).

- **DORA 2024 "verification tax" framing**, cited by Opslane: time saved writing code is re-spent auditing it. Well-supported (Accelerate report has broad practitioner uptake), but the "verification tax" label appears to be Opslane's coinage applied to DORA data, not DORA's own term.

---

### 2. Agent Feedback Loop Pattern — Tiered vs. Full-Suite

**Well-supported (primary source, Anthropic's own docs):**

Claude Code's official best-practices guide ([code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices)) does **not** explicitly prescribe tiered loops (fast inner-loop / full-suite pre-commit). Instead it recommends:

- Give the agent *any* verifiable check (tests, build exit code, linter, diff script) so the loop closes autonomously. The check can be a targeted single test, not the whole suite.
- CLAUDE.md example line cited verbatim: `"Prefer running single tests, and not the whole test suite, for performance"` — this is the clearest Anthropic guidance toward targeted/fast inner-loop testing.
- Four escalating gate options: inline prompt, `/goal` condition, Stop hook (deterministic gate), verification subagent (adversarial reviewer). The Stop hook is the strongest — blocks turn-end until the check passes, up to 8 consecutive blocks.
- Adversarial subagent pattern: a second Claude in a fresh context reviews the diff against requirements, not the reasoning that produced it. Recommended before marking unattended runs done.

**Implied tiered pattern (not explicitly named as such):** The guidance to "run single tests for performance" in inner loops, combined with Stop hooks for pre-commit gates, maps onto the tiered-loop model in practice — but Anthropic does not publish it as a named pattern.

---

### 3. Concrete Techniques — What Practitioners Advocate

**Go test caching (moderately well-supported):**
- [Rotational Labs: Speeding Up Go Tests](https://rotational.io/blog/speeding-up-go-tests/) and [bjorn.now Go test cache on CI](https://bjorn.now/blog/2025/07/07/working-with-gos-test-cache-on-ci/): caching `GOCACHE` on CI is an easy win. Key caveat: ~10% of tests may not cache as expected in complex codebases; black-box integration tests hitting APIs can cache incorrectly. Known Go issue: ModTime-dependent cache misses on CI ([golang/go#58571](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/58571)).
- `-short` flag and affected-test selection are not covered in these sources with practitioner case studies; their use is implied but anecdotal.

**Shifting test pyramid shape (anecdotal, vendor-influenced):**
- [Bug0 blog](https://bug0.com/blog/software-testing-strategies) and [Frontiers journal: Test Pyramid 2.0](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/artificial-intelligence/articles/10.3389/frai.2025.1695965/full) argue the pyramid should become a "trapezoid" — more E2E, fewer integration tests — because AI agents can run thousands of parallel browser sessions cheaply. E2E cost dropped an order of magnitude. Confidence: low-to-medium; driven by AI testing vendors; limited independent empirical data.

**Structural enforcement over advisory checks:**
- Opslane and the search aggregate data both note: "36% of practitioners using AI code generation skip QA entirely" — structural enforcement (hooks that cannot be bypassed) is the only reliable solution. Corroborated by Claude Code's Stop hook design, which blocks Claude from ending a turn until the check passes.

**Mutation/property testing:** No credible 2025–2026 practitioner source surfaced advocating these as an agent-specific technique. Not covered.

---

### Confidence Summary

| Claim | Confidence |
|---|---|
| Verification (not coding speed) is the binding constraint | High — multiple independent data points (Agoda, Faros AI, DORA framing, Opslane) |
| AI-written tests share AI code blind spots | Medium — reasonable but lacks large empirical study |
| CLAUDE.md guidance: prefer single tests over full suite in inner loop | High — direct primary source, Anthropic |
| Stop hook as deterministic pre-commit gate | High — Anthropic docs |
| Go test caching on CI as a concrete speedup | Medium — practitioner posts, but known cache-miss edge cases |
| Trapezoid over pyramid (more E2E, fewer integration) | Low — vendor-positioned, minimal independent evidence |
| METR: AI made devs 19% slower | Anecdotal — single study, contested |

---

**Actionable summary:** The well-evidenced recommendation is: use targeted tests (single package or affected subset) as the inner-loop signal so the agent iterates quickly; gate pre-commit on a deterministic hook running the full relevant suite; use a separate adversarial subagent as the final reviewer before merging. Anthropic's docs endorse this structure implicitly; no external practitioner source packages it as a named "tiered loop" pattern.

**Guard mechanism recommendation: `testing.Short()` over a build tag.**

The codebase already uses `testing.Short()` as the convention (`sqlite_contention_test.go` sets the template; `observe/otel/receiver` follows it). A build tag (`//go:build integration`) is already used for the two truly expensive end-to-end tests (`serve_global_proxy_test.go`, `session_roundtrip_test.go`) that compile the binary and drive the full server stack. The natural split is: use `testing.Short()` for tests that are slow but share a package with fast tests (since they cannot be in a separate file cleanly without splitting packages), and reserve `//go:build integration` for tests that require a pre-built binary or an external service. Adding `if testing.Short() { t.Skip(...) }` at the top of each identified slow test, then running `go test -short ./...` as the default CI gate, matches what the codebase has already established. **Guard mechanism recommendation: `testing.Short()` over a build tag.**

The codebase already uses `testing.Short()` as the convention (`sqlite_contention_test.go` sets the template; `observe/otel/receiver` follows it). A build tag (`//go:build integration`) is already used for the two truly expensive end-to-end tests (`serve_global_proxy_test.go`, `session_roundtrip_test.go`) that compile the binary and drive the full server stack. The natural split is: use `testing.Short()` for tests that are slow but share a package with fast tests (since they cannot be in a separate file cleanly without splitting packages), and reserve `//go:build integration` for tests that require a pre-built binary or an external service. Adding `if testing.Short() { t.Skip(...) }` at the top of each identified slow test, then running `go test -short ./...` as the default CI gate, matches what the codebase has already established. ## Raw Findings Per Question

### CODEX CLI

**Q1. Non-interactive modes: flags, JSON output, session persistence, transcript paths**

Source: https://developers.openai.com/codex/noninteractive

- Command: `codex exec <prompt>`
- `--json`: outputs JSON Lines to stdout. Each line is an event object.
- `--ephemeral`: prevents persisting session rollout files to disk (inverse: without this flag, session state is persisted)
- `-o <path>` / `--output-last-message <path>`: writes final agent message to a file
- `--output-schema <path>`: requests structured JSON response conforming to schema
- `--ignore-user-config`: skips `$CODEX_HOME/config.toml`
- `--sandbox <level>`: `read-only` (default), `workspace-write`, `danger-full-access`

**Emitted event types in `--json` mode:**
```
{"type":"thread.started","thread_id":"..."}
{"type":"turn.started"}
{"type":"item.started","item":{"id":"...","type":"...","status":"..."}}
{"type":"item.completed","item":{"id":"...","type":"...","text":"..."}}
{"type":"turn.completed","usage":{"input_tokens":...,"output_tokens":...}}
```
Item types include: agent messages, reasoning, command executions, file changes, MCP tool calls, web searches, plan updates.

**Standard mode (no `--json`):**
- Progress streams to stderr
- Final agent message printed to stdout only

**Session persistence:**
- `codex exec resume [SESSION_ID]` or `codex exec resume --last` resumes previous sessions
- `history.persistence` config key: `save-all` or `none`
- `history.max_bytes`: caps history file size
- Without `--ephemeral`, session rollout files are written to disk (exact path undocumented in retrieved content; `sqlite_home` config key sets directory for the SQLite state database)

---

**Q2. Codex CLI lifecycle hooks — do they fire in exec mode?**

Source: https://developers.openai.com/codex/hooks

Hook events supported:
- `SessionStart`, `SubagentStart`, `SubagentStop`
- `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`
- `PermissionRequest`
- `PreCompact`, `PostCompact`
- `UserPromptSubmit`
- `Stop`

Registration locations (all loaded if present):
- `~/.codex/hooks.json` (user layer)
- `~/.codex/config.toml` (user layer)
- `<repo>/.codex/hooks.json` (project layer)
- `<repo>/.codex/config.toml` (project layer)
- Plugin-bundled `hooks/hooks.json`
- Enterprise `requirements.toml`

**Do hooks fire in exec mode?** The documentation does not explicitly distinguish. It mentions `--dangerously-bypass-hook-trust` for "one-off automation," which implies hooks operate in exec/non-interactive contexts. The `notify` config key also fires a command with a JSON payload notification — this appears exec-mode compatible. No explicit confirmation or denial found.

**Payload format:**
- All hooks receive JSON on stdin with: `session_id`, `cwd`, `hook_event_name`, `model`
- Exit code `0` = success
- Exit code `2` = blocking decision (with reason in stderr)
- `Stop` and `SubagentStop` require JSON on stdout (not plain text)

---

**Q3. Codex as MCP server**

Source: https://developers.openai.com/codex/guides/agents-sdk

Documented and fully supported:

```bash
codex mcp-server
```

Inspect with: `npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector codex mcp-server`

**Two exposed tools:**
1. `codex` — initiates a session. Params: `prompt` (required), `approval-policy`, `sandbox`, `model`, `config`
2. `codex-reply` — continues existing conversation. Params: `prompt` (required), `threadId` (required)

**Integration pattern (OpenAI Agents SDK):**
```python
async with MCPServerStdio(
    name="Codex CLI",
    params={"command": "codex", "args": ["mcp-server"]},
    client_session_timeout_seconds=360000,
) as codex_mcp_server:
    agent = Agent(name="Developer", mcp_servers=[codex_mcp_server])
```

**Hook behavior in MCP server mode:** Not documented. The MCP server mode exposes `codex` and `codex-reply` as tools; whether hooks installed in `~/.codex/` fire during tool execution is unspecified.

---

### GEMINI CLI

**Q4. Headless mode (`gemini -p`) — do extensions/hooks load? Where are transcripts?**

Source: https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/main/docs/cli/headless.md (404 — page not found)

Fallback from `docs/extensions/reference.md` fetch:

Headless mode activates in non-TTY environments or via `-p`/`--prompt` flag.

**Output formats via `--output-format`:**
- JSON: single object with `response`, `stats`, `error`
- Streaming JSON (JSONL): events `init`, `message`, `tool_use`, `tool_result`, `error`, `result`

**Exit codes:** 0 success, 1 general error, 42 input error, 53 turn limit exceeded

**Whether extensions/hooks load in headless:** The headless.md doc (404) did not load. The extensions reference doc explicitly states: "The documentation does not explicitly address whether extensions and their hooks load in headless or non-interactive mode." — this is a documentation gap.

**Transcript paths:** Not documented in retrieved content.

---

**Q5. Gemini CLI hooks — events, registration, headless behavior**

Source: https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/main/docs/hooks/index.md

**11 lifecycle events:**
1. `SessionStart` — session begins (startup, resume, clear)
2. `SessionEnd` — session ends (exit, clear)
3. `BeforeAgent` — after user submits prompt, before planning; can block turns
4. `AfterAgent` — agent loop ends; allows retry/halt
5. `BeforeModel` — before LLM request; can modify prompts
6. `AfterModel` — after LLM response; enables filtering/redaction
7. `BeforeToolSelection` — before tool selection; can filter available tools
8. `BeforeTool` — before tool executes; can block dangerous operations
9. `AfterTool` — after tool executes
10. `PreCompress` — before context compression (advisory only)
11. `Notification` — system notifications (advisory)

**Registration:** `settings.json` files, merged from layers: project (`.gemini/settings.json`), user (`~/.gemini/settings.json`), system (`/etc/gemini-cli/settings.json`), extensions.

**Do hooks fire in headless mode?** The hook docs explicitly do not specify. A separate "Hooks reference" document is cited for "definitive technical specification of I/O schemas" — that doc returned 404. **Status: undocumented/unconfirmed.**

---

**Q6. ACP mode (`--acp`)**

No ACP documentation was found in any retrieved Gemini CLI doc. The `docs/acp.md` path returned 404. The extensions reference and subagents doc contain no mention of ACP. This is either an internal/unreleased feature, the path has moved, or the acronym differs from what was assumed.

**Status: not found in current public documentation.**

---

**Q7. Can Gemini CLI act as an MCP server?**

Source: https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/main/docs/core/subagents.md

"The document does not indicate Gemini CLI acts as an MCP server itself — it only consumes MCP tools through subagents via the `mcpServers` configuration."

Gemini CLI extensions can define `mcpServers` in their manifest: "These servers will be loaded on startup just like MCP servers defined in a `settings.json` file." This means Gemini CLI is an MCP *consumer*, not an MCP *server*.

**Status: Gemini CLI cannot serve as an MCP server. No documented MCP server mode exists.**

---

### CLAUDE CODE ORCHESTRATION

**Claude Code non-interactive / external CLI orchestration**

Source: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless

Claude Code has a documented programmatic mode (`claude -p`) with:
- `--output-format stream-json`: JSONL event stream (same model as Codex's `--json`)
- `--bare`: skips hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, memory — clean for CI
- `--continue` / `--resume <session-id>`: session persistence across calls
- `--agents <json>`: inject custom agent definitions at invocation time
- `--mcp-config <file-or-json>`: inject MCP servers without project config

**Cleanest pattern for Claude orchestrating a non-Claude CLI agent:**

The documented pattern is: wrap the external CLI as an MCP server, then pass it to Claude via `--mcp-config`. Codex supports this natively (`codex mcp-server`). Claude Code can then call `codex` and `codex-reply` tools as if they were any other MCP tool.

For Gemini CLI (no MCP server mode), the only documented pattern is wrapping it in a Bash tool call — Claude runs `gemini -p "..."` as a subprocess, parses stdout. This loses hook observability entirely.

---

## Feasibility Matrix

| Mode | Live hooks (wipnote observes in real time) | Transcript ingest (post-hoc) | Wrapper launcher only |
|---|---|---|---|
| **codex exec `--json`** | Likely yes — hooks fire in exec mode (inferred from `--dangerously-bypass-hook-trust` for "one-off automation"; not explicitly confirmed). wipnote hooks in `~/.codex/hooks.json` or `.codex/hooks.json` would load unless `--ignore-user-config` is passed | Yes — JSONL on stdout + session rollout files on disk (path from `sqlite_home`/`log_dir` config); parseable without hook access | Yes — wrapper can capture stdout JSONL |
| **codex mcp-server** | Unknown — whether hooks in `~/.codex/` fire during MCP tool invocations is undocumented. The MCP interface exposes `codex`/`codex-reply` tools; there is no documented hook bridge | No transcript path documented for MCP server mode | Partially — wrapper launching `codex mcp-server` can intercept stdio but MCP is a bidirectional protocol, not a log stream |
| **gemini headless (`gemini -p`)** | Unknown — whether hooks registered in `.gemini/settings.json` fire in headless mode is explicitly not documented | Partial — `--output-format stream-json` produces JSONL on stdout; no session transcript path documented | Yes — wrapper captures stdout JSONL; hook behavior unclear |
| **gemini acp** | Not applicable — no public ACP documentation found | Not applicable | Not applicable |
| **gemini mcp** | Not applicable — Gemini CLI has no MCP server mode; it only consumes MCP | Not applicable | Not applicable |

**Legend — documentation status:**
- "Likely yes" = behavior strongly implied by docs but not stated explicitly
- "Unknown" = docs exist but the specific question is not addressed
- "Not applicable" = feature does not exist or is not publicly documented

---

## Summary

**Actionable finding:** Codex exec (`codex exec --json`) is the strongest programmatic integration path for wipnote observability — it emits a documented JSONL event stream on stdout, supports session resume, and hooks in `.codex/hooks.json` very likely fire (inferred; one confirmation fetch of the full hooks doc would remove the "likely"). The `codex mcp-server` mode is the cleanest orchestration interface for Claude-as-orchestrator, but hook behavior inside MCP invocations is undocumented. Gemini CLI has no MCP server mode, and whether its hooks fire in headless `gemini -p` runs is an explicit documentation gap — transcript ingest via stdout JSONL is the only confirmed observation path. ACP mode in Gemini CLI has no current public documentation and should be treated as non-existent until a source is found.</result>

## Raw Findings Per Question

### CODEX CLI

**Q1. Non-interactive modes: flags, JSON output, session persistence, transcript paths**

Source: https://developers.openai.com/codex/noninteractive

- Command: `codex exec <prompt>`
- `--json`: outputs JSON Lines to stdout. Each line is an event object.
- `--ephemeral`: prevents persisting session rollout files to disk (inverse: without this flag, session state is persisted)
- `-o <path>` / `--output-last-message <path>`: writes final agent message to a file
- `--output-schema <path>`: requests structured JSON response conforming to schema
- `--ignore-user-config`: skips `$CODEX_HOME/config.toml`
- `--sandbox <level>`: `read-only` (default), `workspace-write`, `danger-full-access`

**Emitted event types in `--json` mode:**
```
{"type":"thread.started","thread_id":"..."}
{"type":"turn.started"}
{"type":"item.started","item":{"id":"...","type":"...","status":"..."}}
{"type":"item.completed","item":{"id":"...","type":"...","text":"..."}}
{"type":"turn.completed","usage":{"input_tokens":...,"output_tokens":...}}
```
Item types include: agent messages, reasoning, command executions, file changes, MCP tool calls, web searches, plan updates.

**Standard mode (no `--json`):**
- Progress streams to stderr
- Final agent message printed to stdout only

**Session persistence:**
- `codex exec resume [SESSION_ID]` or `codex exec resume --last` resumes previous sessions
- `history.persistence` config key: `save-all` or `none`
- `history.max_bytes`: caps history file size
- Without `--ephemeral`, session rollout files are written to disk (exact path undocumented in retrieved content; `sqlite_home` config key sets directory for the SQLite state database)

---

**Q2. Codex CLI lifecycle hooks — do they fire in exec mode?**

Source: https://developers.openai.com/codex/hooks

Hook events supported:
- `SessionStart`, `SubagentStart`, `SubagentStop`
- `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`
- `PermissionRequest`
- `PreCompact`, `PostCompact`
- `UserPromptSubmit`
- `Stop`

Registration locations (all loaded if present):
- `~/.codex/hooks.json` (user layer)
- `~/.codex/config.toml` (user layer)
- `<repo>/.codex/hooks.json` (project layer)
- `<repo>/.codex/config.toml` (project layer)
- Plugin-bundled `hooks/hooks.json`
- Enterprise `requirements.toml`

**Do hooks fire in exec mode?** The documentation does not explicitly distinguish. It mentions `--dangerously-bypass-hook-trust` for "one-off automation," which implies hooks operate in exec/non-interactive contexts. The `notify` config key also fires a command with a JSON payload notification — this appears exec-mode compatible. No explicit confirmation or denial found.

**Payload format:**
- All hooks receive JSON on stdin with: `session_id`, `cwd`, `hook_event_name`, `model`
- Exit code `0` = success
- Exit code `2` = blocking decision (with reason in stderr)
- `Stop` and `SubagentStop` require JSON on stdout (not plain text)

---

**Q3. Codex as MCP server**

Source: https://developers.openai.com/codex/guides/agents-sdk

Documented and fully supported:

```bash
codex mcp-server
```

Inspect with: `npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector codex mcp-server`

**Two exposed tools:**
1. `codex` — initiates a session. Params: `prompt` (required), `approval-policy`, `sandbox`, `model`, `config`
2. `codex-reply` — continues existing conversation. Params: `prompt` (required), `threadId` (required)

**Integration pattern (OpenAI Agents SDK):**
```python
async with MCPServerStdio(
    name="Codex CLI",
    params={"command": "codex", "args": ["mcp-server"]},
    client_session_timeout_seconds=360000,
) as codex_mcp_server:
    agent = Agent(name="Developer", mcp_servers=[codex_mcp_server])
```

**Hook behavior in MCP server mode:** Not documented. The MCP server mode exposes `codex` and `codex-reply` as tools; whether hooks installed in `~/.codex/` fire during tool execution is unspecified.

---

### GEMINI CLI

**Q4. Headless mode (`gemini -p`) — do extensions/hooks load? Where are transcripts?**

Source: https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/main/docs/cli/headless.md (404 — page not found)

Fallback from `docs/extensions/reference.md` fetch:

Headless mode activates in non-TTY environments or via `-p`/`--prompt` flag.

**Output formats via `--output-format`:**
- JSON: single object with `response`, `stats`, `error`
- Streaming JSON (JSONL): events `init`, `message`, `tool_use`, `tool_result`, `error`, `result`

**Exit codes:** 0 success, 1 general error, 42 input error, 53 turn limit exceeded

**Whether extensions/hooks load in headless:** The headless.md doc (404) did not load. The extensions reference doc explicitly states: "The documentation does not explicitly address whether extensions and their hooks load in headless or non-interactive mode." — this is a documentation gap.

**Transcript paths:** Not documented in retrieved content.

---

**Q5. Gemini CLI hooks — events, registration, headless behavior**

Source: https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/main/docs/hooks/index.md

**11 lifecycle events:**
1. `SessionStart` — session begins (startup, resume, clear)
2. `SessionEnd` — session ends (exit, clear)
3. `BeforeAgent` — after user submits prompt, before planning; can block turns
4. `AfterAgent` — agent loop ends; allows retry/halt
5. `BeforeModel` — before LLM request; can modify prompts
6. `AfterModel` — after LLM response; enables filtering/redaction
7. `BeforeToolSelection` — before tool selection; can filter available tools
8. `BeforeTool` — before tool executes; can block dangerous operations
9. `AfterTool` — after tool executes
10. `PreCompress` — before context compression (advisory only)
11. `Notification` — system notifications (advisory)

**Registration:** `settings.json` files, merged from layers: project (`.gemini/settings.json`), user (`~/.gemini/settings.json`), system (`/etc/gemini-cli/settings.json`), extensions.

**Do hooks fire in headless mode?** The hook docs explicitly do not specify. A separate "Hooks reference" document is cited for "definitive technical specification of I/O schemas" — that doc returned 404. **Status: undocumented/unconfirmed.**

---

**Q6. ACP mode (`--acp`)**

No ACP documentation was found in any retrieved Gemini CLI doc. The `docs/acp.md` path returned 404. The extensions reference and subagents doc contain no mention of ACP. This is either an internal/unreleased feature, the path has moved, or the acronym differs from what was assumed.

**Status: not found in current public documentation.**

---

**Q7. Can Gemini CLI act as an MCP server?**

Source: https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/main/docs/core/subagents.md

"The document does not indicate Gemini CLI acts as an MCP server itself — it only consumes MCP tools through subagents via the `mcpServers` configuration."

Gemini CLI extensions can define `mcpServers` in their manifest: "These servers will be loaded on startup just like MCP servers defined in a `settings.json` file." This means Gemini CLI is an MCP *consumer*, not an MCP *server*.

**Status: Gemini CLI cannot serve as an MCP server. No documented MCP server mode exists.**

---

### CLAUDE CODE ORCHESTRATION

**Claude Code non-interactive / external CLI orchestration**

Source: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless

Claude Code has a documented programmatic mode (`claude -p`) with:
- `--output-format stream-json`: JSONL event stream (same model as Codex's `--json`)
- `--bare`: skips hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, memory — clean for CI
- `--continue` / `--resume <session-id>`: session persistence across calls
- `--agents <json>`: inject custom agent definitions at invocation time
- `--mcp-config <file-or-json>`: inject MCP servers without project config

**Cleanest pattern for Claude orchestrating a non-Claude CLI agent:**

The documented pattern is: wrap the external CLI as an MCP server, then pass it to Claude via `--mcp-config`. Codex supports this natively (`codex mcp-server`). Claude Code can then call `codex` and `codex-reply` tools as if they were any other MCP tool.

For Gemini CLI (no MCP server mode), the only documented pattern is wrapping it in a Bash tool call — Claude runs `gemini -p "..."` as a subprocess, parses stdout. This loses hook observability entirely.

---

## Feasibility Matrix

| Mode | Live hooks (wipnote observes in real time) | Transcript ingest (post-hoc) | Wrapper launcher only |
|---|---|---|---|
| **codex exec `--json`** | Likely yes — hooks fire in exec mode (inferred from `--dangerously-bypass-hook-trust` for "one-off automation"; not explicitly confirmed). wipnote hooks in `~/.codex/hooks.json` or `.codex/hooks.json` would load unless `--ignore-user-config` is passed | Yes — JSONL on stdout + session rollout files on disk (path from `sqlite_home`/`log_dir` config); parseable without hook access | Yes — wrapper can capture stdout JSONL |
| **codex mcp-server** | Unknown — whether hooks in `~/.codex/` fire during MCP tool invocations is undocumented. The MCP interface exposes `codex`/`codex-reply` tools; there is no documented hook bridge | No transcript path documented for MCP server mode | Partially — wrapper launching `codex mcp-server` can intercept stdio but MCP is a bidirectional protocol, not a log stream |
| **gemini headless (`gemini -p`)** | Unknown — whether hooks registered in `.gemini/settings.json` fire in headless mode is explicitly not documented | Partial — `--output-format stream-json` produces JSONL on stdout; no session transcript path documented | Yes — wrapper captures stdout JSONL; hook behavior unclear |
| **gemini acp** | Not applicable — no public ACP documentation found | Not applicable | Not applicable |
| **gemini mcp** | Not applicable — Gemini CLI has no MCP server mode; it only consumes MCP | Not applicable | Not applicable |

**Legend — documentation status:**
- "Likely yes" = behavior strongly implied by docs but not stated explicitly
- "Unknown" = docs exist but the specific question is not addressed
- "Not applicable" = feature does not exist or is not publicly documented

---

## Summary

**Actionable finding:** Codex exec (`codex exec --json`) is the strongest programmatic integration path for wipnote observability — it emits a documented JSONL event stream on stdout, supports session resume, and hooks in `.codex/hooks.json` very likely fire (inferred; one confirmation fetch of the full hooks doc would remove the "likely"). The `codex mcp-server` mode is the cleanest orchestration interface for Claude-as-orchestrator, but hook behavior inside MCP invocations is undocumented. Gemini CLI has no MCP server mode, and whether its hooks fire in headless `gemini -p` runs is an explicit documentation gap — transcript ingest via stdout JSONL is the only confirmed observation path. ACP mode in Gemini CLI has no current public documentation and should be treated as non-existent until a source is found.</result>

<result>I now have a complete and precise picture of the bug. Here is the diagnosis.

---

## Root Cause Diagnosis — feat-cecb2f2b

### (1) Exact root cause with file:line references

The bug is a **session-ID mismatch between the two separate Bash invocations**. The session ID resolved by `wipnote check --gate` differs from the session ID resolved by the subsequent `wipnote feature complete <id>`, causing `LatestGateRecordForSession` to return no row for the `complete` invocation's session ID.

**Execution path:**

`cmd/wipnote/check.go:67` — `wipnote check --gate` resolves `sessionID` via:
```go
sessionID := hooks.EnvSessionID("")
```

`cmd/wipnote/workitem.go:239-240` — `wipnote feature complete` resolves it via:
```go
sessionID := hooks.EnvSessionID("")
```

Both call the identical three-step fallback in `core/hooks/runner.go:305-325`:
1. `agent.NormaliseSessionID(eventSessionID)` — empty string since there is no CloudEvent; always falls through.
2. `os.Getenv("WIPNOTE_SESSION_ID")` — the env var.
3. `ReadActiveSession(projectDir)` — reads `.wipnote/.active-session`.

**The discriminating condition:** the symptom report states `.wipnote/.active-session` is a git-tracked runtime file that churns between calls. The `WriteActiveSession` function (`core/hooks/session_start.go:43`) is called by the `SessionStart` hook whenever a new Claude session starts. If the orchestrator dispatches the two invocations as **separate Bash tool calls** (which are separate subprocesses), and a `SessionStart` hook fires between them (e.g. because the orchestrator opens a new subagent or the tool-spawned subprocess triggers a session event), then `.wipnote/.active-session` will be **overwritten with a different session ID** between the two calls.

**The mismatch is specifically**:

- `wipnote check --gate` runs, reads `WIPNOTE_SESSION_ID=<SESSION_A>` (or falls through to `.active-session` which contains `<SESSION_A>`). It persists a `GateRecord` in SQLite with `session_id = SESSION_A`.
- Between calls: the orchestrator's Bash tool spawns a new subprocess (or a SessionStart hook fires), and `.active-session` is overwritten with `SESSION_B` (the researcher/orchestrator agent's own session ID, or the new invocation's session).
- `wipnote feature complete <id>` runs, `WIPNOTE_SESSION_ID` is absent (each Bash tool call starts fresh with no inherited shell state), and falls through to `.active-session` which now contains `SESSION_B`.
- `LatestGateRecordForSession(database, SESSION_B)` returns `nil` (no record for SESSION_B).
- `sessionScopedValid` is `false`.
- The cross-session fallback `LatestPassingGateRecordForWorkItem` then queries by `work_item_id` AND `status='pass'` — but the `GateRecord` written by `wipnote check --gate` may have `work_item_id = ""` (empty) if `activeWorkItemForGate` returned empty for that call, making the cross-session fallback also fail.

The **chained invocation** (`wipnote check --gate && wipnote feature complete <id>`) succeeds because both halves run **within a single shell process**, so `WIPNOTE_SESSION_ID` if exported by a parent shell, or `.active-session` if read once, is the same for both. More critically, no new `SessionStart` hook fires between `&&`-chained commands within one process, so `.active-session` is not overwritten between reads.

**Failing predicate** (`core/db/gate_records.go:62-67`):
```go
func (gr *GateRecord) SignatureValid() bool {
    if gr == nil || strings.TrimSpace(gr.Signature) == "" {
        return false
    }
    return gr.Signature == gr.ComputeSignature()
}
```
But before `SignatureValid()` is even checked, the guard is:
```go
record, err := dbpkg.LatestGateRecordForSession(database, sessionID)
sessionScopedValid := record != nil && record.Status == "pass" && record.SignatureValid()
```
`record` is `nil` (no row for SESSION_B), so `sessionScopedValid = false`. Then the fallback at line 581:
```go
fallback, ferr := dbpkg.LatestPassingGateRecordForWorkItem(database, workItemID, completionGateFallbackWindow)
```
This also returns `nil` or a non-qualifying record because either (a) the original gate record has `work_item_id = ""` (activeWorkItemForGate returned empty for SESSION_A), or (b) a genuine work-item ID mismatch, or (c) the 6-hour recency window is satisfied but `SignatureValid()` fails.

**The signature is not the cause of drift.** `ComputeSignature()` depends only on fields stored in the DB row itself (`SessionID`, `WorkItemID`, `Harness`, `ProjectType`, `GateCommand`, `Status`, `CheckedAt` UTC, `AllowlistHitsJSON`, `Source`, `OutputSummary`). None of those change between writes and reads. The signature round-trips cleanly.

**The actual root cause is that `WIPNOTE_SESSION_ID` is not exported into the environment of separate Bash subprocess calls.** Each orchestrator Bash tool call is a child process with its own environment. The only persistent mechanism is `.active-session`, and that file is overwritten by `WriteActiveSession` whenever a SessionStart hook fires in any concurrent session (each hook call is a separate process writing atomically via rename).

There is a **second contributing factor**: `activeWorkItemForGate` (`check_gate_support.go:502-520`) queries `GetActiveWorkItemWithFallback(database, sessionID, agentID)`. If the `sessionID` for the `check --gate` call differs from what `complete` will use, the `work_item_id` stored in the gate record may be the actual work item (SESSION_A owns the active item) while the fallback query uses a different `workItemID` (possibly empty string if the `complete` invocation's `sessionID` doesn't own the active item in the DB).

However, re-reading `wiSetStatusWithAgent` (`workitem.go:310`):
```go
} else if err := checkCompletionGateRecord(p.DB, filepath.Dir(dir), sessionID, id); err != nil {
```
The `workItemID` passed to `validateCompletionGateRecord` is `id` (the explicit CLI argument), not a lookup. So the cross-session fallback at `LatestPassingGateRecordForWorkItem(database, workItemID, ...)` queries using the correct explicit work item ID.

**Therefore, the cross-session fallback should work — but only if the gate record itself has a matching non-empty `work_item_id`.** The gate record written by `wipnote check --gate` has `workItemID = activeWorkItemForGate(sessionID, agentID)`. If SESSION_A's DB entry doesn't have an active work item attributed (possible if the Bash subprocess doesn't inherit `WIPNOTE_SESSION_ID`), `workItemID` is `""`, and `InsertGateRecord` stores `NULL` via `nullStr("")`. Then `LatestPassingGateRecordForWorkItem` queries `WHERE work_item_id = '<feat-id>'` and gets no match.

**The complete failure chain:**

1. `wipnote check --gate` runs in Bash tool call #1. `WIPNOTE_SESSION_ID` not in env (not exported from parent shell or cleared). Falls through to `.active-session`, reads `SESSION_A`.
2. `activeWorkItemForGate(SESSION_A, agentID)` returns `""` because SESSION_A has no active work item in the DB (the actual item is attributed to SESSION_B in `active_work_items`, since SESSION_B is the orchestrator's session that ran `wipnote feature start <id>`).
3. Gate record is persisted: `session_id=SESSION_A`, `work_item_id=""` (null).
4. Between calls, SessionStart fires or `.active-session` is overwritten to `SESSION_B`.
5. `wipnote feature complete <id>` runs in Bash tool call #2. Falls to `.active-session`, reads `SESSION_B`.
6. `LatestGateRecordForSession(db, SESSION_B)` → nil (no record for SESSION_B).
7. `LatestPassingGateRecordForWorkItem(db, "feat-<id>", 6h)` → nil (the only `pass` record has `work_item_id=""`, not `"feat-<id>"`).
8. Error: "refusing to complete: no valid passing gate record exists..."

### (2) Minimal fix proposal

The fix must not weaken the "HEAD-changed re-gate" semantics from bug-35857288. The immediate re-check at the end of `validateCompletionGateRecord` is what enforces HEAD currency; the precondition check is just a guard against running `complete` without having ever run `check --gate`.

**Fix option A (preferred, minimal):** In `check_gate_support.go:267-353` (`runSessionGate`), when `workItemID` is empty (not resolved from the current session's active work item), accept the work item ID passed as an explicit argument to the gate rather than storing `""`. The gate call already receives `workItemID` as a parameter — the issue is `activeWorkItemForGate` returning `""`. The fix is to make `persistGateRecord` (and therefore `runSessionGate`) accept the work item ID from the caller when `activeWorkItemForGate` returns empty:

In `check.go:69-70`, the `--gate` code path already calls `activeWorkItemForGate(sessionID, agentID)` and passes the result. The caller doesn't know the work item ID at that point. The gap is that the orchestrator should pass the work item ID explicitly when it knows it.

**Fix option B (more robust):** Make `checkCompletionGateRecord` pass the explicit work item ID to `runSessionGate` via `validateCompletionGateRecord`. This already happens for the re-check (`runSessionGate` at line 592 gets `workItemID` from `validateCompletionGateRecord`'s parameter). But the precondition query `LatestGateRecordForSession` is session-scoped, not work-item-scoped. Change the precondition to prefer `LatestPassingGateRecordForWorkItem` when there is a known `workItemID`:

```go
// In validateCompletionGateRecord, change the sessionScoped lookup to also
// accept a record for the same work_item_id from any recent session:
record, err := dbpkg.LatestGateRecordForWorkItemOrSession(database, sessionID, workItemID)
```

This is essentially promoting the cross-session fallback to the primary lookup, but scoped to the correct work item.

**Fix option C (simplest, addresses the root cause directly):** In `check --gate` (`check.go:69`), accept an explicit `--work-item <id>` flag. The orchestrator already knows which work item it is gating. Pass it explicitly rather than relying on the DB lookup `activeWorkItemForGate`. This way the gate record always has the correct `work_item_id` regardless of which session is "active" at call time.

Fix C requires an orchestrator-level prompt change (or agent behavior) to pass the flag. Fix A/B are code-only.

**Fix B is the minimal code fix** with the lowest blast radius: change `validateCompletionGateRecord` so that when `LatestGateRecordForSession` returns nil (or a failing record), it immediately attempts `LatestPassingGateRecordForWorkItem` — which already exists and is already called — but the cross-session fallback already does this at `check_gate_support.go:581`. The actual problem is that the cross-session fallback returns nil because `work_item_id` was stored as `""` in the gate record.

**Root fix:** Ensure that `work_item_id` in the gate record is always non-empty when the gate is run with intent to gate a specific work item. This requires passing the work item ID to `wipnote check --gate` explicitly (as an optional flag) or deriving it from a session-independent lookup (e.g., the `.wipnote/.active-session` file's attributed work item, or the most recently started in-progress item).

### (3) Volatile paths to exclude from signature

The signature is **not the cause of the failure**. `signablePayload()` includes only fields stored in the DB row that were set at insert time and never change. No volatile file paths (`debug.log`, `.active-session`) appear anywhere in the signature inputs. The signature is:

```
SessionID + WorkItemID + Harness + ProjectType + GateCommand + Status + CheckedAt (UTC RFC3339Nano) + AllowlistHitsJSON + Source + OutputSummary
```

None of these change between write and read. `ProfileSignature` and `GuardsRunJSON` are explicitly excluded from `signablePayload` (they are stored but not signed — see the comment at `gate_records.go:26-34`). No volatile paths need to be excluded; the signature is not drifting.

### (4) Confidence and confirming experiment

**Confidence: HIGH** (8/10). The session-ID mismatch path is unambiguous from the code. The remaining uncertainty is whether SESSION_A and SESSION_B are always different in practice — it depends on whether `.active-session` is actually overwritten between the two Bash calls, or whether `WIPNOTE_SESSION_ID` is simply absent in both subprocess environments.

**Confirming experiment (describe, don't run):**

Run `wipnote check --gate` in isolation and observe the printed session ID and work item ID. Then immediately run `wipnote feature complete <id>` and note what session ID it resolves. Compare:

```bash
WIPNOTE_DEBUG=1 wipnote check --gate 2>&1 | grep -E "session|gate|work.item"
WIPNOTE_DEBUG=1 wipnote feature complete feat-cecb2f2b 2>&1 | grep -E "session|gate|work.item"
```

If the session IDs differ between the two printouts, this confirms the mismatch hypothesis. A secondary check: after the failing `check --gate`, inspect the SQLite gate record directly:

```bash
sqlite3 ~/.cache/wipnote/*/wipnote.db "SELECT session_id, work_item_id, status, signature FROM gate_records ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 3;"
```

If `work_item_id` is empty (`NULL`/`""`) for the most recent `pass` record, that confirms the second contributing factor (empty work_item_id prevents the cross-session fallback from matching).

---

**Actionable summary:** The completion gate fails because `wipnote check --gate` resolves a different session ID than `wipnote feature complete` (each is a separate Bash subprocess with no `WIPNOTE_SESSION_ID` in env; `.active-session` may be overwritten between calls by a SessionStart hook) AND stores `work_item_id=""` in the gate record (because `activeWorkItemForGate` finds no DB attribution for the transient session ID), so neither the session-scoped lookup nor the work-item cross-session fallback in `validateCompletionGateRecord` can match the record. Fix: require `wipnote check --gate` to accept an explicit work item ID flag so the gate record always carries a non-empty `work_item_id` that the cross-session fallback can match.</result>

## Root Cause Diagnosis — feat-cecb2f2b

### (1) Exact root cause with file:line references

The bug is a **session-ID mismatch between the two separate Bash invocations**. The session ID resolved by `wipnote check --gate` differs from the session ID resolved by the subsequent `wipnote feature complete <id>`, causing `LatestGateRecordForSession` to return no row for the `complete` invocation's session ID.

**Execution path:**

`cmd/wipnote/check.go:67` — `wipnote check --gate` resolves `sessionID` via:
```go
sessionID := hooks.EnvSessionID("")
```

`cmd/wipnote/workitem.go:239-240` — `wipnote feature complete` resolves it via:
```go
sessionID := hooks.EnvSessionID("")
```

Both call the identical three-step fallback in `core/hooks/runner.go:305-325`:
1. `agent.NormaliseSessionID(eventSessionID)` — empty string since there is no CloudEvent; always falls through.
2. `os.Getenv("WIPNOTE_SESSION_ID")` — the env var.
3. `ReadActiveSession(projectDir)` — reads `.wipnote/.active-session`.

**The discriminating condition:** the symptom report states `.wipnote/.active-session` is a git-tracked runtime file that churns between calls. The `WriteActiveSession` function (`core/hooks/session_start.go:43`) is called by the `SessionStart` hook whenever a new Claude session starts. If the orchestrator dispatches the two invocations as **separate Bash tool calls** (which are separate subprocesses), and a `SessionStart` hook fires between them (e.g. because the orchestrator opens a new subagent or the tool-spawned subprocess triggers a session event), then `.wipnote/.active-session` will be **overwritten with a different session ID** between the two calls.

**The mismatch is specifically**:

- `wipnote check --gate` runs, reads `WIPNOTE_SESSION_ID=<SESSION_A>` (or falls through to `.active-session` which contains `<SESSION_A>`). It persists a `GateRecord` in SQLite with `session_id = SESSION_A`.
- Between calls: the orchestrator's Bash tool spawns a new subprocess (or a SessionStart hook fires), and `.active-session` is overwritten with `SESSION_B` (the researcher/orchestrator agent's own session ID, or the new invocation's session).
- `wipnote feature complete <id>` runs, `WIPNOTE_SESSION_ID` is absent (each Bash tool call starts fresh with no inherited shell state), and falls through to `.active-session` which now contains `SESSION_B`.
- `LatestGateRecordForSession(database, SESSION_B)` returns `nil` (no record for SESSION_B).
- `sessionScopedValid` is `false`.
- The cross-session fallback `LatestPassingGateRecordForWorkItem` then queries by `work_item_id` AND `status='pass'` — but the `GateRecord` written by `wipnote check --gate` may have `work_item_id = ""` (empty) if `activeWorkItemForGate` returned empty for that call, making the cross-session fallback also fail.

The **chained invocation** (`wipnote check --gate && wipnote feature complete <id>`) succeeds because both halves run **within a single shell process**, so `WIPNOTE_SESSION_ID` if exported by a parent shell, or `.active-session` if read once, is the same for both. More critically, no new `SessionStart` hook fires between `&&`-chained commands within one process, so `.active-session` is not overwritten between reads.

**Failing predicate** (`core/db/gate_records.go:62-67`):
```go
func (gr *GateRecord) SignatureValid() bool {
    if gr == nil || strings.TrimSpace(gr.Signature) == "" {
        return false
    }
    return gr.Signature == gr.ComputeSignature()
}
```
But before `SignatureValid()` is even checked, the guard is:
```go
record, err := dbpkg.LatestGateRecordForSession(database, sessionID)
sessionScopedValid := record != nil && record.Status == "pass" && record.SignatureValid()
```
`record` is `nil` (no row for SESSION_B), so `sessionScopedValid = false`. Then the fallback at line 581:
```go
fallback, ferr := dbpkg.LatestPassingGateRecordForWorkItem(database, workItemID, completionGateFallbackWindow)
```
This also returns `nil` or a non-qualifying record because either (a) the original gate record has `work_item_id = ""` (activeWorkItemForGate returned empty for SESSION_A), or (b) a genuine work-item ID mismatch, or (c) the 6-hour recency window is satisfied but `SignatureValid()` fails.

**The signature is not the cause of drift.** `ComputeSignature()` depends only on fields stored in the DB row itself (`SessionID`, `WorkItemID`, `Harness`, `ProjectType`, `GateCommand`, `Status`, `CheckedAt` UTC, `AllowlistHitsJSON`, `Source`, `OutputSummary`). None of those change between writes and reads. The signature round-trips cleanly.

**The actual root cause is that `WIPNOTE_SESSION_ID` is not exported into the environment of separate Bash subprocess calls.** Each orchestrator Bash tool call is a child process with its own environment. The only persistent mechanism is `.active-session`, and that file is overwritten by `WriteActiveSession` whenever a SessionStart hook fires in any concurrent session (each hook call is a separate process writing atomically via rename).

There is a **second contributing factor**: `activeWorkItemForGate` (`check_gate_support.go:502-520`) queries `GetActiveWorkItemWithFallback(database, sessionID, agentID)`. If the `sessionID` for the `check --gate` call differs from what `complete` will use, the `work_item_id` stored in the gate record may be the actual work item (SESSION_A owns the active item) while the fallback query uses a different `workItemID` (possibly empty string if the `complete` invocation's `sessionID` doesn't own the active item in the DB).

However, re-reading `wiSetStatusWithAgent` (`workitem.go:310`):
```go
} else if err := checkCompletionGateRecord(p.DB, filepath.Dir(dir), sessionID, id); err != nil {
```
The `workItemID` passed to `validateCompletionGateRecord` is `id` (the explicit CLI argument), not a lookup. So the cross-session fallback at `LatestPassingGateRecordForWorkItem(database, workItemID, ...)` queries using the correct explicit work item ID.

**Therefore, the cross-session fallback should work — but only if the gate record itself has a matching non-empty `work_item_id`.** The gate record written by `wipnote check --gate` has `workItemID = activeWorkItemForGate(sessionID, agentID)`. If SESSION_A's DB entry doesn't have an active work item attributed (possible if the Bash subprocess doesn't inherit `WIPNOTE_SESSION_ID`), `workItemID` is `""`, and `InsertGateRecord` stores `NULL` via `nullStr("")`. Then `LatestPassingGateRecordForWorkItem` queries `WHERE work_item_id = '<feat-id>'` and gets no match.

**The complete failure chain:**

1. `wipnote check --gate` runs in Bash tool call #1. `WIPNOTE_SESSION_ID` not in env (not exported from parent shell or cleared). Falls through to `.active-session`, reads `SESSION_A`.
2. `activeWorkItemForGate(SESSION_A, agentID)` returns `""` because SESSION_A has no active work item in the DB (the actual item is attributed to SESSION_B in `active_work_items`, since SESSION_B is the orchestrator's session that ran `wipnote feature start <id>`).
3. Gate record is persisted: `session_id=SESSION_A`, `work_item_id=""` (null).
4. Between calls, SessionStart fires or `.active-session` is overwritten to `SESSION_B`.
5. `wipnote feature complete <id>` runs in Bash tool call #2. Falls to `.active-session`, reads `SESSION_B`.
6. `LatestGateRecordForSession(db, SESSION_B)` → nil (no record for SESSION_B).
7. `LatestPassingGateRecordForWorkItem(db, "feat-<id>", 6h)` → nil (the only `pass` record has `work_item_id=""`, not `"feat-<id>"`).
8. Error: "refusing to complete: no valid passing gate record exists..."

### (2) Minimal fix proposal

The fix must not weaken the "HEAD-changed re-gate" semantics from bug-35857288. The immediate re-check at the end of `validateCompletionGateRecord` is what enforces HEAD currency; the precondition check is just a guard against running `complete` without having ever run `check --gate`.

**Fix option A (preferred, minimal):** In `check_gate_support.go:267-353` (`runSessionGate`), when `workItemID` is empty (not resolved from the current session's active work item), accept the work item ID passed as an explicit argument to the gate rather than storing `""`. The gate call already receives `workItemID` as a parameter — the issue is `activeWorkItemForGate` returning `""`. The fix is to make `persistGateRecord` (and therefore `runSessionGate`) accept the work item ID from the caller when `activeWorkItemForGate` returns empty:

In `check.go:69-70`, the `--gate` code path already calls `activeWorkItemForGate(sessionID, agentID)` and passes the result. The caller doesn't know the work item ID at that point. The gap is that the orchestrator should pass the work item ID explicitly when it knows it.

**Fix option B (more robust):** Make `checkCompletionGateRecord` pass the explicit work item ID to `runSessionGate` via `validateCompletionGateRecord`. This already happens for the re-check (`runSessionGate` at line 592 gets `workItemID` from `validateCompletionGateRecord`'s parameter). But the precondition query `LatestGateRecordForSession` is session-scoped, not work-item-scoped. Change the precondition to prefer `LatestPassingGateRecordForWorkItem` when there is a known `workItemID`:

```go
// In validateCompletionGateRecord, change the sessionScoped lookup to also
// accept a record for the same work_item_id from any recent session:
record, err := dbpkg.LatestGateRecordForWorkItemOrSession(database, sessionID, workItemID)
```

This is essentially promoting the cross-session fallback to the primary lookup, but scoped to the correct work item.

**Fix option C (simplest, addresses the root cause directly):** In `check --gate` (`check.go:69`), accept an explicit `--work-item <id>` flag. The orchestrator already knows which work item it is gating. Pass it explicitly rather than relying on the DB lookup `activeWorkItemForGate`. This way the gate record always has the correct `work_item_id` regardless of which session is "active" at call time.

Fix C requires an orchestrator-level prompt change (or agent behavior) to pass the flag. Fix A/B are code-only.

**Fix B is the minimal code fix** with the lowest blast radius: change `validateCompletionGateRecord` so that when `LatestGateRecordForSession` returns nil (or a failing record), it immediately attempts `LatestPassingGateRecordForWorkItem` — which already exists and is already called — but the cross-session fallback already does this at `check_gate_support.go:581`. The actual problem is that the cross-session fallback returns nil because `work_item_id` was stored as `""` in the gate record.

**Root fix:** Ensure that `work_item_id` in the gate record is always non-empty when the gate is run with intent to gate a specific work item. This requires passing the work item ID to `wipnote check --gate` explicitly (as an optional flag) or deriving it from a session-independent lookup (e.g., the `.wipnote/.active-session` file's attributed work item, or the most recently started in-progress item).

### (3) Volatile paths to exclude from signature

The signature is **not the cause of the failure**. `signablePayload()` includes only fields stored in the DB row that were set at insert time and never change. No volatile file paths (`debug.log`, `.active-session`) appear anywhere in the signature inputs. The signature is:

```
SessionID + WorkItemID + Harness + ProjectType + GateCommand + Status + CheckedAt (UTC RFC3339Nano) + AllowlistHitsJSON + Source + OutputSummary
```

None of these change between write and read. `ProfileSignature` and `GuardsRunJSON` are explicitly excluded from `signablePayload` (they are stored but not signed — see the comment at `gate_records.go:26-34`). No volatile paths need to be excluded; the signature is not drifting.

### (4) Confidence and confirming experiment

**Confidence: HIGH** (8/10). The session-ID mismatch path is unambiguous from the code. The remaining uncertainty is whether SESSION_A and SESSION_B are always different in practice — it depends on whether `.active-session` is actually overwritten between the two Bash calls, or whether `WIPNOTE_SESSION_ID` is simply absent in both subprocess environments.

**Confirming experiment (describe, don't run):**

Run `wipnote check --gate` in isolation and observe the printed session ID and work item ID. Then immediately run `wipnote feature complete <id>` and note what session ID it resolves. Compare:

```bash
WIPNOTE_DEBUG=1 wipnote check --gate 2>&1 | grep -E "session|gate|work.item"
WIPNOTE_DEBUG=1 wipnote feature complete feat-cecb2f2b 2>&1 | grep -E "session|gate|work.item"
```

If the session IDs differ between the two printouts, this confirms the mismatch hypothesis. A secondary check: after the failing `check --gate`, inspect the SQLite gate record directly:

```bash
sqlite3 ~/.cache/wipnote/*/wipnote.db "SELECT session_id, work_item_id, status, signature FROM gate_records ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 3;"
```

If `work_item_id` is empty (`NULL`/`""`) for the most recent `pass` record, that confirms the second contributing factor (empty work_item_id prevents the cross-session fallback from matching).

---

**Actionable summary:** The completion gate fails because `wipnote check --gate` resolves a different session ID than `wipnote feature complete` (each is a separate Bash subprocess with no `WIPNOTE_SESSION_ID` in env; `.active-session` may be overwritten between calls by a SessionStart hook) AND stores `work_item_id=""` in the gate record (because `activeWorkItemForGate` finds no DB attribution for the transient session ID), so neither the session-scoped lookup nor the work-item cross-session fallback in `validateCompletionGateRecord` can match the record. Fix: require `wipnote check --gate` to accept an explicit work item ID flag so the gate record always carries a non-empty `work_item_id` that the cross-session fallback can match.</result>

feat: add --work-item flag and last-resort fallback to wipnote check --gate (feat-cecb2f2b)

Gate records were stored with empty work_item_id when the CLI subprocess's
session ID differed from the session that started the work item (concurrent
agent SessionStart hooks overwrote .active-session). The cross-session fallback
in LatestPassingGateRecordForWorkItem cannot match records with empty
work_item_id, forcing redundant full re-runs.

- Add optional --work-item <id> flag to `wipnote check --gate`; when provided
  it takes precedence over session-resolved attribution for the gate record.
- Add resolveGateWorkItem() with 3-level resolution: (1) explicit flag,
  (2) session-scoped claim via activeWorkItemForGate, (3) last-resort
  MostRecentInProgressWorkItem query. Logs the resolution path to stderr.

- Tests: TestPersistGateRecord_ExplicitWorkItemID, TestResolveGateWorkItem_*,
  TestValidateCompletionGateRecord_CrossSessionMatchByWorkItemID,
  TestMostRecentInProgressWorkItem.

fix: canonical-first finalize gate + reindex replay for slice approvals (bug-eca8141d)

IsPlanFullyApproved now accepts optional YAML slice descriptors so it can
fall back to ApprovalStatus/Approved fields when plan_feedback has no rows
(cache rebuild / first-run scenario). planFinalizeHandler and parsePlanListItem
pass the loaded YAML slices through. The defense-in-depth check in
planFinalizeHandler mirrors the same fallback for per-slice status.

reindexPlanApprovals replays YAML-baked slice approvals into plan_feedback
using INSERT OR IGNORE, keeping live interactive rows authoritative. It is
called from runReindex (full reindex path only) so every cache rebuild is
self-healing.

Six tests added: canonical fallback true/false, DB rows override YAML,
reindex replays approvals, INSERT OR IGNORE preserves live rows, and
pending slices are not replayed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
)"","description":"Commit the fix"}
